title: The Capuchins (1528)
hookLine: a reform with hoods, beards and poverty; Padre Pio was one

lines: A BEARD, A HOOD, BARE FEET.
cards: In old paintings of the saints, some friars look wilder than the rest: a full beard, a long pointed hood, bare feet in sandals, a rough habit patched where it wore through. That's on purpose.

Inside the family of Francis, a group of brothers came to believe the order had drifted from the poverty he loved. They wanted to go back: to hermitages and begging, to preaching in plain words to plain people.
They took up a hood shaped the way they believed Francis wore his, and people gave them a nickname for it. Today's word is that nickname.

teach.b: Capuchin. Tradition says the name comes from the Italian word for that hood. The street chose it, and it stuck.

teach.h: LIVE THE RULE WITHOUT THE COMFORTS.
teach.b: What they wanted was simple and hard: to live the Rule of Francis without the comforts that had crept in. Smaller houses, fewer things, long hours of silent prayer, then out among ordinary people.
The early years weren't easy. The reform had opponents inside the Franciscan family, and for a time it wasn't clear it would survive.

teach.h: STILL FRANCISCANS: ONE BRANCH, ONE TREE.
teach.b: It did, and it stayed in the family: Capuchins are Franciscans, one branch of the same tree, following the same Rule. Tradition remembers them staying when sickness came to a town, nursing the dying when others fled.
You met one Capuchin back on day nine hundred five: Padre Pio, in southern Italy, whom the Church honors as Saint Pio of Pietrelcina.

teach.h: PADRE PIO AND THE LONG LINES.
teach.b: People traveled from far away to stand in long lines for his confessional. There were reports that he bore wounds like Christ's, and the Church looked into them with care and caution.
But what drew people was often simpler: a poor friar in a brown hood who would listen to the worst thing you had done.

It echoes Jesus in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." The reform kept pointing at the same thing: go back to the poor man of Assisi, and then go out.

how: Capuchin friars live in community under the Rule of Saint Francis, and are often found in parishes, soup kitchens, hospitals and confessionals; Catholics who are devoted to Saint Pio of Pietrelcina often ask his prayers.

games.why: the Capuchins chose a reform inside the family: smaller houses, fewer things, more prayer, and then out to the people. they stayed Franciscans.

practice: Picture one Capuchin somewhere today, in a soup line, a hospital corridor, a confessional with the little light on, waiting for whoever comes.
Then bring to mind someone in your own life who listens to other people's burdens, a nurse, a counselor, a priest, a friend everyone calls.
If you pray, pray for the Capuchins and for that person, in your own words or with an Our Father; if not, just hold them both kindly.

wordCard.voice: Capuchin. A Franciscan reform that went back to poverty and prayer, named, tradition says, for its hood. Padre Pio wore it. Today's word.

orig.note: Italian: a hood. tradition ties the friars' nickname to it.

carryVoice: Your line: the hooded friars. A beard, a hood, and a door left open for the burdened. Until tomorrow.
